newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gle des Eaux steps up UK rail drive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gle des Eaux steps up UK rail drive.

text.p: LONDON - French utility group Generale des Eaux took over its second London regional rail franchise on Monday, pledging to restore confidence in the railways.
Halfway through the privatisation of Britain's 25 train operating companies, Generale des Eaux has won two of the busiest through its CGEA transport branch.
At the weekend it took control of South Eastern and added it to South Central, which it took over in July, giving a combined annual turnover of about 600 million pounds ($947 million).
CGEA director Antoine Hurel will be the new chief executive of Connex Rail -- the new corporate identity that the two networks will share.
"We are launching Connex as a sign of our commitment," he told an industry and media audience.
He said "the most startling aspect" of the 15-year South Eastern franchise was Connex's agreement to spend several hundred million pounds on replacing ageing trains.
Critics of the privatisation process have said in the past that the relatively short duration of government franchise contracts would make large-scale fleet replacement impossible.
Hurel said later that Connex was also in bid negotiations with the rail franchising office OPRAF for some of the other train operating companies still to be franchised.
Managers at South Central said they were also in talks with OPRAF -- in their case trying to extend their franchise to 15 years from seven to let them replace trains.

"Customers want new trains, therefore we have started discussions with OPRAF to see if there is a way to get a 15 year franchise," South Central managing director Geoff Harrison-Mee said. "A 15-year franchise means new trains."

Connex faces a challenge to recover customers in both of its franchise catchment areas, which run from Kent in south east England along the Channel coast to Hampshire in the west, and cover many parts of southeast and south London.
Hurel said the company wanted to use the opportunity of privatisation to reverse the decline in rail useage and restore public confidence in trains.
As well as South Eastern's new trains, the two lines also plan to upgrade stations, information systems and security, and each promises to improve service levels under the Connex brand.
Hurel said Connex had to find a way of improving customer quality in a way that rewarded shareholders yet also responded to the taxpayer.

As in all franchise contracts, both lines will initially receive an annual subsidy payment from the state, channeled through OPRAF, in return for which they have to provide closely-regulated levels of service and fares.

In the case of South Eastern, with its longer franchise period and a stated aim to improve efficiency and cut costs as well as enhancing revenue, the company will not need a subsidy in the final year of its contract.

Its subsidy is set to fall from 125.4 million pounds ($198 million) in 1996/97 to 5.7 million pounds in 12 year's time, nil the following year, and in the final year South Eastern should pay a 2.6 million premium to the state. ($1=.6337 Pound)
